content: 1. For the treatment of tinea infections, topical antifungal agents such as clotrimazole or miconazole should be initiated for a duration of three to four weeks. This recommendation is strong, although the evidence supporting it is of low quality. 2. In cases of extensive tinea infections or involvement of hair and nails in both children and adults, oral griseofulvin should be considered. This is a conditional recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. 3. If there is no response to initial treatment, oral terbinafine or itraconazole should be used as alternative therapies. This is also a conditional recommendation with very low-quality evidence. 4. For children and adults with tinea infections and unknown HIV status, an HIV test should be offered. This is a strong recommendation, though the evidence is of low quality. 5. In HIV-infected individuals (children, adolescents, and adults, including pregnant women) with herpes zoster, acyclovir is recommended to prevent disease dissemination and promote resolution at any stage of the disease. This is a strong recommendation with low-quality evidence. 6. All individuals presenting with herpes zoster and unknown HIV status should be offered an HIV test. If the test is positive, they should be assessed for antiretroviral therapy (ART) eligibility. This is a strong recommendation with low-quality evidence. 7. For mild to moderate scabies in HIV-infected individuals, including pregnant women, topical permethrin 5% (applied twice) is recommended. If permethrin is unavailable, benzyl benzoate (at least two applications) should be used. 8. If there is poor response to treatment or permethrin is not feasible, oral ivermectin at a dose of 200 µg/kg is recommended. This is a strong recommendation with low-quality evidence. 9. For severe or crusted scabies in HIV-infected individuals weighing ≥15 kg, two doses of oral ivermectin (spaced one to two weeks apart) are recommended. If ivermectin is unavailable, topical permethrin 5% or benzyl benzoate should be used until clinical clearance is achieved. Longer treatment durations may be required. This is a conditional recommendation with very low-quality evidence. 10. For severe or crusted scabies in HIV-infected children weighing <15 kg, topical permethrin 5% or benzyl benzoate should be used until clinical clearance is achieved. Additionally, a keratolytic agent such as 5% salicylic acid can be used to remove scale bulk. This is a conditional recommendation with very low-quality evidence. 11. For extensive or unusually distributed molluscum contagiosum in HIV-infected patients, ART should be considered as the primary treatment. No additional specific treatment is recommended. This is a conditional recommendation with very low-quality evidence. 12. Adults presenting with new-onset molluscum contagiosum in high HIV-prevalence settings and unknown HIV status should be offered an HIV test. If positive, they should be assessed for ART eligibility. This is a strong recommendation with low-quality evidence. 13. Prompt initiation of ART is recommended for all HIV-infected individuals (adults, adolescents, and children, including pregnant and breastfeeding women) with oropharyngeal candidiasis. This is a strong recommendation with high-quality evidence. 14. In HIV-infected individuals with Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis, the suspected causative drug should be promptly discontinued, and supportive therapies should be provided. This is a strong recommendation with very low-quality evidence. 15. The use of systemic corticosteroids in Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis is not recommended. This is a conditional recommendation with very low-quality evidence. 16. HIV-infected children with severe acute malnutrition (SAM) who qualify for lifelong ART should be started on ART as soon as possible after stabilization of metabolic complications and sepsis. Stabilization is indicated by the return of appetite and resolution of severe edema. These children should receive the same ART regimens and doses as HIV-infected children without SAM. Close monitoring is required during the first six to eight weeks of ART initiation to identify early metabolic complications and opportunistic infections. This is a strong recommendation with very low-quality evidence. 17. HIV-infected children with SAM should be managed with the same therapeutic feeding approaches as HIV-uninfected children with SAM. This is a strong recommendation with very low-quality evidence. 18. HIV-infected children with SAM should receive a high dose of vitamin A upon admission (50,000 IU to 200,000 IU depending on age) and zinc for diarrhea management unless they are already receiving fortified therapeutic feeds (F75, F100, or RUTF) that meet WHO specifications. This is a strong recommendation with very low-quality evidence. 19. Persistent diarrhea in HIV-infected children with SAM that does not resolve with standard management should be investigated for carbohydrate intolerance and infectious causes requiring different management, such as fluid and feed modifications or antibiotics. This is a strong recommendation with very low-quality evidence. 20. For uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria, children and adults (except pregnant women in their first trimester) should be treated with one of the following artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACT): artemether-lumefantrine, artesunate-amodiaquine, artesunate-mefloquine, dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine, or artesunate-sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine. This is a strong recommendation with high-quality evidence. 21. ACT regimens should provide three days of treatment with an artemisinin derivative. For dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine, the daily dose should be 5 mg/kg of dihydroartemisinin and 20 mg/kg of piperaquine for three days. This is a strong recommendation based on pharmacokinetic modeling. 22. To reduce transmission of treated P. falciparum malaria, a single dose of 0.25 mg/kg body weight of primaquine should be added to ACT, except in pregnant women, infants under six months, and breastfeeding women of infants under six months. Testing for glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency is not required. This is a strong recommendation with low-quality evidence. 23. Pregnant women in their first trimester with uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria should be treated with seven days of quinine and clindamycin. This is a strong recommendation. 24. Infants weighing less than 5 kg with uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria should be treated with ACT at the same mg/kg body weight target dose as children weighing 5 kg. This is a strong recommendation. 25. In HIV-infected individuals with uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria, avoid artesunate-sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine if they are being treated with co-trimoxazole, and avoid artesunate-amodiaquine if they are being treated with efavirenz or zidovudine. This is a good practice statement. 26. Non-immune travelers returning to non-endemic settings with uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria should be treated with ACT. This is a strong recommendation with low-quality evidence. 27. Individuals with uncomplicated P. falciparum hyperparasitemia are at increased risk of treatment failure, severe malaria, and death. They should be closely monitored in addition to receiving ACT. This is a good practice statement. 28. For uncomplicated P. vivax, P. ovale, P. malariae, or P. knowlesi malaria, if the species is not known with certainty, treat as for uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria. This is a good practice statement. 29. In areas with chloroquine-susceptible infections, adults and children with uncomplicated P. vivax, P. ovale, P. malariae, or P. knowlesi malaria should be treated with either ACT (except in pregnant women in their first trimester) or chloroquine. This is a strong recommendation with high-quality evidence. 30. In areas with chloroquine-resistant infections, adults and children with uncomplicated P. vivax, P. ovale, P. malariae, or P. knowlesi malaria (except pregnant women in their first trimester) should be treated with ACT. This is a strong recommendation with high-quality evidence. 31. Pregnant women in their first trimester with chloroquine-resistant P. vivax malaria should be treated with quinine. This is a strong recommendation with very low-quality evidence. 32. To prevent relapse in P. vivax or P. ovale malaria, G6PD status should guide the administration of primaquine. This is a good practice statement. 33. For relapse prevention, treat P. vivax or P. ovale malaria with primaquine (0.25 mg/kg body weight daily for 14 days) in all transmission settings. Alternatively, a weekly dose of 0.75 mg/kg body weight for eight weeks may be used under close medical supervision for potential primaquine-induced hemolysis. This is a conditional recommendation with very low-quality evidence. 34. When G6PD status is unknown and testing is unavailable, the decision to prescribe primaquine must be based on an assessment of the risks and benefits. This is a good practice statement. 35. Adults and children with severe malaria (including infants, pregnant women in all trimesters, and lactating women) should be treated with intravenous or intramuscular artesunate for at least 24 hours and until they can tolerate oral medication. Once parenteral therapy is completed, treatment should be finished with three days of ACT. In low-transmission areas, a single dose of primaquine should be added. This is a strong recommendation with high-quality evidence. 36. If artesunate is unavailable, artemether is preferred over quinine for treating severe malaria in children and adults. This is a conditional recommendation with low-quality evidence. 37. For suspected severe malaria cases pending transfer to a higher-level facility, administer a single intramuscular dose of artesunate and refer the patient for further care. If intramuscular artesunate is unavailable, use intramuscular artemether or quinine. For children under six years, a single rectal dose of artesunate (10 mg/kg body weight) may be used, but rectal artesunate should not be used in older children or adults. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-quality evidence. 38. Diagnostic testing and treatment for malaria should be integrated into programs promoting the management of febrile illnesses in both children and adults.
